septic-tank-pumping.metaDescription: Lake Los Angeles, CA septic tank pumping for desert homes and manufactured homes on large lots. We dig out buried lids, pump the tank and explain it.
septic-tank-pumping.heroSub: We pump septic tanks on Lake Los Angeles desert lots, digging out lids that blown sand has buried and checking how each tank feeds its pit or field.
paragraphs: Lake Los Angeles homes sit on private septic almost without exception, so the tank in the yard handles every shower, load of laundry and flush in the house. The community's mix of older site-built houses, manufactured homes and newer construction means tank sizes and ages vary a lot from one lot to the next. A manufactured home placed long ago may drain to a tank that was put in for an earlier owner, and the paperwork rarely survives. Before we settle on a pumping interval for a Lake Los Angeles household, we like to see the tank itself, measure what is inside and learn how big it really is.

Pumping out here usually begins with a shovel. Wind off the open desert drives sand across yards near Saddleback Butte and along the avenues, and a lid that sat at the surface a few years ago may now be under several inches of drift. Once the lid is off, we read the liquid level before the hose goes in, because a tank running high on one of these lots often points to a seepage pit or field slowed by caliche below. Then we pull out the sludge and scum, break up the packed layer on the bottom and look over both baffles.

Lancaster Septic Service is a locally owned and operated company, and the drive east across the valley to Lake Los Angeles is one our crew makes regularly. Give us your cross streets when you call, along with anything we should know about the gate, the dogs or a dirt drive that gets soft after rain. We park within hose reach, keep the work area tidy and fasten the lid so the next windstorm cannot fill the opening with sand. Before we leave, you hear what the tank looked like and when the next pumping should probably happen for the number of people living there.

faqs.q: How often should a Lake Los Angeles household pump its septic tank?
faqs.a: A common guideline is every 3 to 5 years, though many homes here have tanks of unknown size, which makes that range a starting point rather than a rule. A small tank serving a full manufactured home may need service sooner. Our crew measures the sludge and scum at the first visit and suggests an interval based on what we actually find in your tank.

faqs.q: My lid is buried under sand. Do I need to dig it up before you come?
faqs.a: No. Blown sand covering a lid is one of the most common things we run into on Lake Los Angeles lots, and digging down to it is part of the visit. If you have an old stake, a sketch or a rough idea of where the tank sits, share it with us. Many owners here add a riser afterward so the lid stays easy to find.

seepage-pit-pumping.metaDescription: Seepage pit pumping in Lake Los Angeles, California for full or slow pits on desert lots. We pump the pit and tank, then watch how the pit recovers.
seepage-pit-pumping.heroSub: Lake Los Angeles pits often sit above caliche, so we pump them down, watch how fast they recover and tell you how much soaking room is left.
paragraphs: Sandy ground near the surface is common across Lake Los Angeles, but caliche and harder layers tend to show up as you go deeper, and that is exactly where a seepage pit does its work. A pit that reached open, sandy soil can keep draining for a long time. One that ended near a hard layer may fill sooner than the owner expects. Plenty of lots here have a pit working alone, while others pair a pit with a leach field, and some had a second pit added by a past owner with little record of where it went.

Pumping a pit on these lots is part cleanout and part test. Our crew uncovers the pit cap, which drifting sand has often hidden along with the tank lid, and compares the liquid level with the inlet pipe. We usually pump the septic tank on the same trip so fresh solids stop washing over. After the pit is drawn down, we watch how quickly water seeps back through the walls. On a Lake Los Angeles property, slow recovery often means the soil around the lower rings has sealed or the pit is resting on caliche that never let much through.

Locally owned and operated, Lancaster Septic Service makes the trip east for seepage pit work in Lake Los Angeles on a regular basis. Tell us when you call whether the property has one pit, two, or a pit plus a field, and whether the ground over any of them has sunk. Keep trucks and trailers off that area, since old pit caps on open desert lots are not built for weight. After the pump-out, you get a straight answer on whether the pit has life left or whether a new pit should be part of the plan.

faqs.q: Why does my Lake Los Angeles seepage pit fill up faster than my neighbor's?
faqs.a: Soil can change a lot between neighboring desert lots. One pit may have reached deep, sandy ground while the next stopped near caliche or a harder layer that barely lets water through. Pit age, tank pumping history and household size matter too. When we pump your pit, the recovery rate afterward tells us more about your soil than any comparison over the fence.

faqs.q: Will Los Angeles County need to be involved if my pit has to be replaced?
faqs.a: Adding or replacing a seepage pit usually involves Los Angeles County Environmental Health, and the county may require a soil evaluation or a review of the layout before work starts. Requirements vary, so it is worth checking with them early. Our crew can help you understand what the county may require for a Lake Los Angeles lot and how that fits with pumping in the meantime.

septic-inspection.metaDescription: Septic inspections in Lake Los Angeles, CA for escrow and owners with no records. We open the tank, check the pit or field and explain the results.
septic-inspection.heroSub: Many Lake Los Angeles systems were added to over the years with little paperwork, so our inspections start by working out what is really in the ground.
paragraphs: Buying a home in Lake Los Angeles often means buying a septic system nobody can fully describe. Many systems here were added to or rebuilt over the years, and the only record may be a faded receipt in a kitchen drawer. A manufactured home on a large lot might drain to an older tank, a newer pit, or both, and the listing rarely says which. That uncertainty is a big part of why buyers and lenders often ask for an inspection during escrow here, and why sellers who order one early tend to have an easier time answering questions.

An inspection on these lots covers more ground than the tank alone. Our crew locates the tank, often digging through drifted sand to reach the lid, then measures the sludge and scum, checks the baffles and notes the tank size and material. We run water through the house to see how it arrives and whether anything flows back from the outlet. Then we find the seepage pit or leach field, and sometimes both, and look for standing water, odors or soggy patches on flat ground where storm water tends to collect.

Sale timelines matter, so give us the escrow dates and the agent's contact when you book, and let us know whether the house will have running water on the day of the visit. Lancaster Septic Service is locally owned and operated, and we treat Lake Los Angeles inspections as a chance to hand the next owner a clear picture of the layout along with the findings. You get a written summary in plain language. Requirements around property sales may vary, so check with your agent and Los Angeles County Environmental Health about what applies to your transaction.

faqs.q: Is an inspection worth it on a Lake Los Angeles home that is not being sold?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many owners here bought without seeing the tank or knowing whether the house drains to a pit, a field or both. An inspection answers those questions, shows how full the tank is, and flags baffles or a disposal area that are starting to struggle. It is also a sensible step before adding a bedroom, a second unit or more people to the household.

faqs.q: The seller says the system was rebuilt. How will we know what was done?
faqs.a: Paperwork may exist with Los Angeles County Environmental Health, and it is worth asking the seller for any receipts or drawings. On the ground, our crew can usually tell whether there is more than one pit, whether a field was added, and how the parts connect. We describe what we can see and what we cannot confirm, so you know where the open questions are before escrow closes.

septic-repair.metaDescription: Septic system repair in Lake Los Angeles, CA for broken baffles, cracked lids and damaged lines on older desert systems. Quote before any work.
septic-repair.heroSub: Heat, cold nights and decades of patchwork take a toll on Lake Los Angeles systems. We find the one part that failed and fix it.
paragraphs: Summer heat in Lake Los Angeles bakes the ground hard around a septic tank, and cold winter nights can leave shallow lines sluggish. Those swings, plus years of gases working on older concrete tanks, are hard on baffles, lids and the pipes that connect the house to the system. Many homes here have systems that were patched or extended by past owners, so a repair call sometimes turns up a fitting or a section of pipe that was never meant to be permanent. A slow drain on one of these lots can trace back to any part between the house and the seepage pit or field.

Pinpointing the failed part comes first. Our crew opens the tank, looks at the liquid level and the baffles, and runs a camera through a line if the trouble seems to be in the pipe. On a large Lake Los Angeles lot, the run between the house and the tank can be long, and a vehicle path or a trailer parked over it for years can crack or separate the pipe. Once we know what broke, we explain the fix and give you a quote before digging. Typical jobs include a new baffle or sanitary tee, a replacement lid, or a cut-out pipe section.

Share a few details when you call, such as which drains are slow, whether the trouble comes and goes with the weather, and whether anything heavy has been driven or parked near the tank. Lancaster Septic Service is locally owned and operated, and we would rather fix the single part that failed on a Lake Los Angeles system than talk you into work you do not need. Some repairs may involve Los Angeles County requirements, and we can help you understand what may apply. Either way, you see the plan and the quote before a shovel touches your yard.

faqs.q: Can cold winter nights in Lake Los Angeles really affect my septic system?
faqs.a: They can. Lines that sit close to the surface cool down on cold nights, and waste can move more slowly through them, especially if the pipe already has a sag or a partial clog. A properly buried, sloped line usually handles the cold fine. If your drains slow down mostly in winter, our crew can look at the line depth and condition and tell you whether a repair makes sense.

faqs.q: Does a repair on an older Lake Los Angeles system need county approval?
faqs.a: Simple fixes like a new baffle or a cracked lid may not need much beyond the work itself, while larger repairs usually involve more steps. Los Angeles County Environmental Health may require a review or an inspection for some jobs, and requirements vary. We can help you understand what the county may require for your repair before any work starts, so the process holds no surprises.

leach-field-repair.metaDescription: Leach field repair in Lake Los Angeles, CA for flat desert lots where storms and caliche leave fields soggy. We find the cause and fix what failed.
leach-field-repair.heroSub: When a storm leaves your flat Lake Los Angeles lot soggy over the trenches, we trace why the field stopped draining and explain the fix.
paragraphs: Flat desert lots are common in Lake Los Angeles, and that flatness is a mixed blessing for a leach field. Trenches are easy to lay out, but when a heavy storm finally comes through, rainwater has nowhere to run off and can sit over the field until the soil is soaked. A field that was already slowing down from years of solids can tip into surfacing effluent after a single storm. Caliche below the trenches makes it worse, holding water close to the surface when it should be soaking down through the sandy ground above it.

Finding why the field stopped absorbing is the real job. We start at the tank, since an overdue pump-out or a broken outlet baffle on a Lake Los Angeles system often sends solids straight into the trenches. Then we open the distribution box, check whether it is level, and probe the field to see which trenches are saturated. A camera can show crushed or clogged laterals. Repairs might mean jetting the lines, resetting the box, resting part of the field, adding trenches in fresh sandy ground, or in some cases moving the disposal area to a seepage pit instead.

Ease off the field while you wait for us by spreading out laundry, fixing running toilets and pointing runoff from gutters or a driveway away from the trenches. Keep vehicles, trailers and stored equipment off the area too. Locally owned and operated, Lancaster Septic Service handles Lake Los Angeles field repairs with an eye on how your particular lot drains, because flat ground and caliche can change the right answer from one parcel to the next. Larger field work may involve Los Angeles County review, and we can help you understand what may be required.

faqs.q: Why does my leach field only act up after a big storm?
faqs.a: On flat Lake Los Angeles lots, heavy rain can soak the ground over the field and leave effluent with nowhere to go. A healthy field usually recovers as the soil dries, but a field already sealing with biomat or sitting over caliche may stay wet much longer. If drains slow after every storm, it is a sign the field is close to its limit and worth having checked.

faqs.q: Is a seepage pit a better choice than a new leach field on my lot?
faqs.a: It depends on your soil. Where caliche sits close to the surface, a deep pit that reaches past it may drain better than shallow trenches, while open sandy ground can suit a field well. Soil testing usually settles the question, and Los Angeles County may require it for a new disposal area. We walk the lot with you and explain which direction makes sense.

septic-installation.metaDescription: Septic installation and replacement in Lake Los Angeles, CA for new homes on open desert lots and worn-out systems. Site visits, layout help and risers.
septic-installation.heroSub: Building on open desert in Lake Los Angeles or replacing a tired system, we help you plan around sandy soil and caliche and install it with care.
paragraphs: Newer homes in Lake Los Angeles sit on open desert lots, including parcels out toward Saddleback Butte State Park, and each one needs its own septic system because there is no sewer line to tie into. Replacement work is just as common on older lots, where a tank or pit added long ago has finally given out. Either way, the design starts with the soil. Sandy ground near the surface can drain well, but caliche and harder layers deeper down can decide whether a leach field or a seepage pit is the better fit for the parcel.

Planning comes before digging. Most parcels need a percolation test or other soil evaluation so the designer knows how quickly water drains at the depth of the future trenches or pit, and Los Angeles County Environmental Health may ask for a design review and inspections before the system is put to use. On a big Lake Los Angeles lot, picture where a garage, a workshop or a future manufactured home might go, since the tank and disposal area need to stay clear of them. A long dirt drive also has to hold up under an excavator and the truck delivering the tank.

The first step is a site visit, where our crew walks the lot, checks setbacks from property lines and any well, and works out how equipment will get from the road to the dig. We can help you sort out what the county may expect and work alongside the people doing the soil testing and design. When installation starts, the tank goes in level on a firm base, the field or pits are built to the approved plan, and risers bring every lid up high enough that drifting sand will not swallow it. Locally owned and operated, Lancaster Septic Service wants your new Lake Los Angeles system to be easy to care for from its first pumping on.

faqs.q: Is soil testing needed before building on a Lake Los Angeles lot?
faqs.a: In most cases, some kind of soil testing is part of planning a new system, and Los Angeles County may require it before approving a design. The results show how quickly water soaks in at the depth where a field or pit would sit, which matters a great deal on lots where caliche turns up below sandy topsoil. Check with Los Angeles County Environmental Health about what applies to your parcel.

faqs.q: My old system was pieced together by past owners. Can it be replaced in stages?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the tank is sound but the pit or field has failed, replacing only the disposal area may be an option, and the reverse can also be true. In other cases, mismatched parts mean a full replacement is the cleaner fix. Our crew looks at each piece and explains what is worth keeping. The county may have its own requirements for partial replacements, so we help you check.

septic-risers.metaDescription: Septic riser and lid installation in Lake Los Angeles, CA. Bring buried lids above the blowing sand with sealed, fastened lids for easier pumping.
septic-risers.heroSub: Blowing sand buries Lake Los Angeles lids within a few seasons. A sealed riser lifts the lid above the drift so every pumping starts without a shovel.
paragraphs: Spring winds in Lake Los Angeles move a surprising amount of sand, and a septic lid at ground level can disappear under a drift within a few seasons. Out near Saddleback Butte State Park, owners often tell us they set a marker over the tank years ago and the marker is gone too. A riser lifts the access point up through that drift so the lid stays visible, and a sealed lid keeps sand and dust from sifting into the tank between pumpings. On a large desert lot with little landscaping to use as a reference, that visibility saves a lot of searching.

Installing risers here usually happens during a pumping visit, since the tank has to be opened anyway. Our crew digs down to each opening, checks the condition of the tank top, and fits a riser adapter before building the riser up in sections. On Lake Los Angeles lots, we often finish the lid a few inches above grade so drifting sand does not bury it again, though some owners prefer it flush. Every joint gets sealed against sand and water, and the lid fastens down so kids, dogs and gusts cannot move it.

Think about where you want the lids before we arrive. If you have a fence line, a gravel pad or a spot where the dogs like to dig, let us know so we can plan around it. As a locally owned and operated company, Lancaster Septic Service puts in risers across Lake Los Angeles for owners who are tired of paying for the same dig every few years. We note the tank location on a simple sketch, and if the tank has never been found, we can locate it during the same trip before the riser work begins.

faqs.q: Will a riser lid stay put during strong Lake Los Angeles winds?
faqs.a: Yes, when it is installed and fastened correctly. The lids we use are heavy and screw or lock down to the riser, so wind cannot lift or slide them. Sealed joints also keep blowing sand from working into the tank. Lids set a few inches above grade tend to stay visible after a windy spell, while flush lids may need a quick sweep now and then.

faqs.q: My tank has two openings. Do both need risers?
faqs.a: Raising both is usually worth it. The main opening is used for pumping, while the outlet side gives access to the baffle or a filter that should be checked during service. On a Lake Los Angeles lot where sand keeps covering things, having both at the surface means nothing has to be dug up again. We look at your tank and suggest what makes sense for it.

grease-trap-pumping.metaDescription: Grease trap pumping in Lake Los Angeles, CA for restaurants and food businesses on septic. Full pump-outs, baffle checks and service records.
grease-trap-pumping.heroSub: Lake Los Angeles kitchens on septic cannot afford escaped grease. We pump the trap fully, check the septic tank too and keep your records current.
paragraphs: Food businesses in and around Lake Los Angeles, from small restaurants and cafes to a market deli counter or a church kitchen that cooks for events, all face fats and oils that harden as soon as they cool. What sets this area apart is that most properties here rely on private septic, so grease that slips past the trap can head straight for a septic tank and then a seepage pit or leach field. Once grease coats sandy soil or the walls of a pit, that soil stops absorbing, and the repair becomes far larger than a routine pump-out.

Our crew pumps the trap or in-ground interceptor completely, scrapes hardened grease from the walls and baffles, and checks the inlet and outlet tees and the lid seal. For a Lake Los Angeles kitchen on septic, we can also look at the septic tank on the same visit, since that is where escaped grease shows up first as a thick scum layer. Visits are planned before opening or after closing so the line is not interrupted, and each pump-out ends with a service record listing the date, what was removed and anything that needs attention.

Pumping frequency depends on trap size, menu and how busy the kitchen gets, and local health agencies may set a schedule or ask to see records. Requirements vary, so ask Los Angeles County Environmental Health what applies to a kitchen like yours. As a locally owned and operated business, we make the drive east across the valley to keep Lake Los Angeles kitchens on a routine that fits their hours. Tell us the trap size and location when you call, and clear the area around the lid before we pull in.

faqs.q: My Lake Los Angeles restaurant is on septic. Does that change how often the grease trap needs pumping?
faqs.a: It can. On sewer, escaped grease clogs public lines. On septic, it collects in your own tank and can seal the seepage pit or field the business depends on. Many kitchens on septic choose to pump the trap more often than they strictly need to, simply to protect the system. We help you set an interval based on your trap size, menu and volume.

faqs.q: Who keeps track of grease trap records for a small kitchen?
faqs.a: The business usually keeps the records, but we make that easy. Every visit comes with a service record showing the date, the trap serviced and what we removed. If Los Angeles County Environmental Health or another agency asks about your grease maintenance, you can hand over the file. Requirements vary, so it is worth asking the county what it may expect for a food business in Lake Los Angeles.

emergency-septic-service.metaDescription: Emergency septic service in Lake Los Angeles, CA for backups, overflows and alarms on desert lots. Call and our crew heads your way as soon as we can.
emergency-septic-service.heroSub: Sewage coming up on your Lake Los Angeles lot after a storm? Call with your road conditions and we head east as soon as we can.
paragraphs: A septic backup in Lake Los Angeles can feel more urgent because the community sits out on the eastern side of the valley, a good distance from central Lancaster. Homes near Avenue M, around the Antelope Valley Indian Museum or out by Saddleback Butte State Park can be well off pavement, and after a rare heavy storm, a dirt road may be soft enough to slow a loaded truck. That same storm is often what caused the trouble in the first place, soaking the ground around a pit or field until the system has nowhere to send water.

Tell us on the phone what you are seeing, where the water is coming up, and how the road and driveway look, so we arrive with the right equipment and a route that works. Our first step on site is to bring the level down by pumping the tank, which usually gets drains flowing again. Then we look for the cause, whether that is a full tank, a clogged inlet line, a broken baffle, or a seepage pit or leach field that has stopped taking water. Once the system is stable, we explain what happened in plain terms.

Until we get there, stop running water in the house, keep kids and dogs away from any sewage inside or in the yard, and open the gate if you can do it safely. If you know where the tank lid is, mark it with something tall, since blown sand often hides lids on Lake Los Angeles lots. Locally owned and operated, Lancaster Septic Service treats a call from out east like any other urgent call and sends a truck your way as soon as we can. Stay by the phone in case the driver needs directions for the last stretch.

faqs.q: Can you reach my Lake Los Angeles home after a storm if my road is dirt?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, but it helps to know what we are driving into. Tell us when you call whether the road or driveway is soft, washed out or blocked, and whether there is a firmer way in. A loaded pump truck is heavy, so we plan the route before heading out. If the truck cannot get close, we can sometimes run extra hose to reach the tank.

faqs.q: Is a backup after heavy rain a sign my system is failing?
faqs.a: Not always. A storm can saturate the soil around a seepage pit or leach field on a flat Lake Los Angeles lot, and a healthy system often recovers as the ground dries. If the backup returns after every storm, or happens in dry weather too, the pit or field may be wearing out. Once the emergency is handled, we explain what we found and what to watch for.

septic-line-jetting.metaDescription: Septic line jetting and camera inspection in Lake Los Angeles, CA. Clear long sewer and leach lines on large desert lots and see the pipe on video.
septic-line-jetting.heroSub: Long lines on big Lake Los Angeles lots can sag, clog and hide old reroutes. We jet them clean and show you the inside on camera.
paragraphs: On a large Lake Los Angeles lot, the pipe from the house to the tank, and on to the seepage pit or field, can be a long run. Sandy soil can shift under that length of pipe and let a section settle into a low spot where waste and grease collect. Lines laid shallow get sluggish on cold winter nights, and older systems that past owners extended or rerouted may have joints that were never lined up well. When a drain keeps clogging no matter how often it is snaked, the answer is usually somewhere along that buried pipe.

Jetting and the camera work together on these systems. Our crew finds a cleanout or opens the tank, then runs the camera first to see what the line looks like and whether it is sound enough for high-pressure water. With the right nozzle, we scour grease, sludge and roots from the full width of the pipe and flush the debris toward the tank. A second camera pass shows the line is clear and reveals any sag, crack or offset joint. If we find damage, we mark its position and depth on the ground so a repair digs in the right place.

Before we arrive, look near the foundation for a cleanout cap and note which drains act up and how often. Since jetting sends debris into the tank, pairing the visit with a pump-out often makes sense, especially if it has been a while. On Lake Los Angeles systems where nobody knows exactly how the lines run, the camera footage from our locally owned and operated crew answers a lot of questions. You watch it with us, and we explain what each problem spot means for your system and your budget.

faqs.q: Can a camera show whether my Lake Los Angeles line was extended by a past owner?
faqs.a: Often it can. Changes in pipe material, odd fittings and joints that do not line up are common signs of an extension or reroute, and the camera shows them clearly. A locator on the camera head also tells us where the line runs and how deep it sits. That is useful on lots here where the layout was never written down or the drawings were lost.

faqs.q: Can jetting help a leach field that floods on my flat lot?
faqs.a: If the laterals are packed with sludge or biomat, jetting can open them back up and spread flow across the field again. It will not fix soil sealed by years of solids or a field sitting over caliche that holds water near the surface. We check the laterals with the camera first, so you know whether jetting is likely to help on your Lake Los Angeles property before you decide.

septic-tank-locating.metaDescription: Septic tank locating in Lake Los Angeles, CA for open desert lots with lost markers and no records. We trace the line, find the tank and mark the lids.
septic-tank-locating.heroSub: No records and no markers on your Lake Los Angeles lot? We trace the line from the house, find the tank and mark the lids.
paragraphs: Open desert lots in Lake Los Angeles offer few clues about where a tank sits. There may be no lawn to show a green patch, no planting bed laid out around the lid, and the markers a past owner left have often been buried or blown away. Add the fact that many systems here were rebuilt or extended over the years without much record, and some buyers end up with a home where nobody can say where the tank is, or whether there is more than one on the property.

We locate tanks by following the sewer line from where it leaves the house. Our crew opens a cleanout, pushes a small transmitter into the pipe and tracks its signal across the lot with a receiver until it stops at the tank inlet, which gives both direction and depth. A steel probe confirms the tank edges, then we dig to the lids. On these lots, we also trace the line beyond the tank when you need it, since knowing where the seepage pit or field sits matters before you add a shed, a carport or a fence.

Gather anything you have before we come, such as a purchase packet, a pumping receipt or a rough sketch, and check whether a cleanout cap near the foundation can be opened. Point out sprinkler lines, a buried water line or anything else we should avoid while probing. Our locally owned and operated crew leaves Lake Los Angeles owners with the lids flagged, measured from fixed points on the house, and drawn on a simple map. Many owners have us add a riser the same day, because a lid found once on open desert ground is easy to lose again after the next windy season.

faqs.q: Can you find a tank on a Lake Los Angeles lot with no records at all?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Electronic tracing from a cleanout or the house plumbing does not depend on paperwork, and probing confirms what the signal shows. Records from Los Angeles County Environmental Health may help if they exist for your parcel, but plenty of tanks here are found without them. It can take a bit longer when the line has been rerouted, but the method still works.

faqs.q: Could my property have more than one septic tank?
faqs.a: It is possible, especially on a large lot that once had a second dwelling or where a past owner added onto the system. Tracing each drain line from the house shows where they go. If two lines lead to two different tanks, we locate and mark both. Knowing this matters during a sale and before any pumping, since an overlooked tank never gets serviced.
